**The text as it arrived.** This is the complete text the run received:

````markdown
---
kntnt:
  genre: opinion
  technique: none
  language: en_GB
---

# Don't switch off Lervik's phone booking before we know what it costs

On 18 June the council executive board is asked to remove phone booking from all seven community venues from September. The officers' report gives one reason: staff should not have to enter the details in two flows. That is a fair thing to want. It is not yet a reason to make the change permanent.

## What the pilot actually counted

The pilot report *Bokning av föreningslokaler*, dated 8 April 2026, covers an eight-week trial in two venues. It records 96 bookings made on the web and 24 made by phone. Those figures are the report's, and so are their limits: it counts bookings rather than unique people, and it measures nothing about age, functional ability or how used to digital services people are. Twenty-four phone bookings therefore cannot tell us what share of Lervik's residents are unable to book digitally. Nobody should claim they can.

## A motive on the table, but no figures under it

The administration's objection to keeping both routes is double administration, and I take it at face value: it is not a claim that people who ring are lazy or expensive. But the documents contain no measurement of how long either route takes staff, and no calculation of what removing one would save. The board is being asked to close a channel for good on the strength of an inconvenience the documents put no number on. That is thin ground for making the change permanent.

## Six months, both routes, and something to measure

Öppna beslut proposes a six-month trial in all seven venues with both booking routes kept open. During it, the administration records the time each booking route takes and asks users to say, voluntarily, why they chose the phone or the web. We make no claim to have funded or costed that trial. What it would cost is for the board to weigh.

A booking made by phone is not proof that somebody cannot use the web. It is a reason to find out why the phone is still being used. I am not against digital booking. I am against settling its shape before the council can set the work each route costs staff against what it is worth to the people who use it.

## What the board can decide on 18 June

Postpone the permanent switch and run the six months with both routes open. When the trial has produced figures, decide whether a channel should be removed, changed or kept. That decision is the board's either way, and it will be a better one for being taken with the cost of both routes on the table.

— Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut
````

Review of input.md. Genre: opinion. Technique: none. Language: en_GB (British English). All three come from the text's own kntnt map. The opinion genre doesn't name a usual technique either. No brief was used.

Findings

1. Unresolved: the lead or the standfirst is missing. Between the headline and the first subheading, the text has one paragraph: "On 18 June the council executive board is asked…". The article anatomy needs a standfirst and a lead that each work on their own. The measuring script reads this paragraph as the standfirst and reports the lead as absent. Whichever one the paragraph is meant to be, the other is missing. What the reader loses: without that paragraph, the body never says what the board is being asked to decide (removing phone booking from all seven community venues from September) before section 2 talks about closing "a channel for good". A missing part is reported, not written, so the author needs to supply it.

2. Unresolved: the opening paragraph doesn't stand on its own as a standfirst. If the opening paragraph is the standfirst, it names "the council executive board" and "the officers' report" but never says which council. Lervik appears only in the headline and later in the body. A reader who sees only the standfirst can't tell which council is deciding. This can only be settled once finding 1 is settled.

3. Repaired: the byline was in the wrong place and form. It was the last line of the text, as "— Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut". It now comes after the opening paragraph and before the first subheading, as "By Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut". What the reader lost: they didn't know who was making the argument until the last line. So in the third section, "Öppna beslut proposes…" and "We make no claim to have funded or costed that trial" reached them before the text had said that Öppna beslut is the author's organisation. The byline sits after the opening paragraph because the measuring script reads that paragraph as the standfirst. If the author turns it into the lead and writes a separate standfirst, the byline belongs between the two.

Anatomy

The text doesn't conform to the article anatomy, because the lead is absent. The other counted limits hold. These parts were checked by reading and meet their requirements: the last section is an ending, with a specific call to action on the board, and each subheading describes its section. How the standfirst and lead work together couldn't be checked, because one of them is missing. Some norms are departed from, but none of these departures is a finding:
- The headline has 12 words and 68 characters. The norm is 3–8 words and at most 60 characters, and 68 is inside the required 20–70. The headline states the argument plainly and every word of it is supported by the text.
- The paragraphs in the first two sections have 85 and 84 words, a little over the 80-word norm. Each holds one thought.
- Five of the six body paragraphs, the opening paragraph included, have four or five sentences, not the usual two or three. The sentences are short and each paragraph is one step of the argument.
I read all five heading pairs, and none repeats the sentence after it.

Claim account

No claim was removed, changed or added. Only the byline moved: it went from the end of the text to after the opening paragraph, and its form changed from a dash to "By". It says the same thing: Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut, is the author.

The byline moved to its place in the article's order and now uses the "By" form. The frontmatter is unchanged. The closing mechanical pass made no corrections. Nothing else in the text changed.

content.content:
## The truth of a report about the text

Everything a run says about a text is true of the text it names. That holds for every statement the reply makes about a text, and not only for its findings and its account of the claims: a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, and what a round did to a passage — moved it, removed it, replaced it, set a heading over it — each tells the reader something about the text they could check, and each is written so that the check holds.

A statement about the delivered text is checked against the delivered text after the last change to it, the closing mechanical pass included. Most of what a run knows about a text it learned while reviewing the text as it arrived, and the rounds changed that text afterwards, so a length measured before a round or a heading remembered from one describes a text the reader is no longer holding. Where a run measures a text with the Collection Library's measuring script, `scripts/article_anatomy.py`, a count or length the reply states is taken from that script's measurement of the text the statement is about, never from the run's own reading of it and never from a measurement of another state of the text. A statement about the text as it arrived says so, so that nobody reads it against the text delivered. A statement that cannot be made true of the text it names is left out.

The check is made on the reply as drafted, one statement at a time, once the text it describes is final, and each statement is read against the passage it names rather than against what the run remembers of it; a finding written during the review is checked in the same way against the text it was written about. A statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere — that a passage is unchanged, word for word what it was or untouched, that the rest of the text was left alone, that a name appears nowhere else, that a heading says nothing about its section — is checked against every part of the text it covers, because a single exception makes it false, and where there is one the statement names it or is narrowed to what holds. A statement of where wording came from, or of where a passage now stands, is checked by finding that passage in the text.

Who reads it decides this too. The reader of a report finds their way in the text by it, and a statement they check and find false costs them the trust they would have given every other statement in the same reply.

======
13:Make the smallest correction that removes a finding. Move or clarify existing material where it supplies the missing connection. Introduce no new evidence, experience, attribution or outcome. If repair would change a claim or a quotation's meaning, or requires information absent from the text, leave the passage and report the unresolved finding. A claim removed because the finding named that claim itself remains part of the claim account, and so does every claim a correction left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, and every claim a correction added — one the corrected text asserts and the text before it has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say. A claim that has a counterpart in the text before is changed rather than added. A headline, a standfirst and a subheading carry claims like any other passage, and a changed claim is accounted for by what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved; a correction that took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text is accounted for by what the reader no longer has, however little of the text went with it. The account is of the text delivered rather than of the text received, and nothing a reviewing Skill says about the claims as a whole contradicts a finding the same reply states.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.

- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

attachment.cliPrefix: You are a Claude agent, built on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

input.command:
diff <(cat <<'EOF'
---
kntnt:
  genre: opinion
  technique: none
  language: en_GB
---

# Don't switch off Lervik's phone booking before we know what it costs

On 18 June the council executive board is asked to remove phone booking from all seven community venues from September. The officers' report gives one reason: staff should not have to enter the details in two flows. That is a fair thing to want. It is not yet a reason to make the change permanent.

## What the pilot actually counted

The pilot report *Bokning av föreningslokaler*, dated 8 April 2026, covers an eight-week trial in two venues. It records 96 bookings made on the web and 24 made by phone. Those figures are the report's, and so are their limits: it counts bookings rather than unique people, and it measures nothing about age, functional ability or how used to digital services people are. Twenty-four phone bookings therefore cannot tell us what share of Lervik's residents are unable to book digitally. Nobody should claim they can.

## A motive on the table, but no figures under it

The administration's objection to keeping both routes is double administration, and I take it at face value: it is not a claim that people who ring are lazy or expensive. But the documents contain no measurement of how long either route takes staff, and no calculation of what removing one would save. The board is being asked to close a channel for good on the strength of an inconvenience the documents put no number on. That is thin ground for making the change permanent.

## Six months, both routes, and something to measure

Öppna beslut proposes a six-month trial in all seven venues with both booking routes kept open. During it, the administration records the time each booking route takes and asks users to say, voluntarily, why they chose the phone or the web. We make no claim to have funded or costed that trial. What it would cost is for the board to weigh.

A booking made by phone is not proof that somebody cannot use the web. It is a reason to find out why the phone is still being used. I am not against digital booking. I am against settling its shape before the council can set the work each route costs staff against what it is worth to the people who use it.

## What the board can decide on 18 June

Postpone the permanent switch and run the six months with both routes open. When the trial has produced figures, decide whether a channel should be removed, changed or kept. That decision is the board's either way, and it will be a better one for being taken with the cost of both routes on the table.

— Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut
EOF
) <(cat <<'EOF'

- **Statement:** "Between the headline and the first subheading, the text has one paragraph: 'On 18 June the council executive board is asked…'." (Finding 1)

A second block, "By Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut", then comes before "## What the pilot actually counted".
  - **What is true:** the delivered text has two blocks between the headline and the first subheading: the opening paragraph and the byline line that the run moved there itself (the measuring script also lists the byline as its own part).
